items.q: The Incas were an ancient ___ that made beautiful gold artefacts.
Gold jewellery is often taken in ___.

One in three adults today will have developed ___ by the time they are sixty.
We now have smart ___ that let us turn appliances on from a distance.

tts: So, what do you think about the first one? — I wouldn’t be surprised if it happened. After all, we can’t all keep flying to places all the time, can we? The planet would get so polluted.
Well, you may be right about that, but I still doubt people would be satisfied with a virtual holiday. I expect they’ll just travel more within their own countries.

I don’t like the sound of a printed meal much, do you? But I think it’s bound to happen. In fact I think they’re already developing the technology. — Really? There’s no chance of me eating something like that.
And what about the last one? — Oh, that’s sure to happen. People will get fed up with being in front of a screen all the time. — Well, yes, I suppose it might happen.

o: Judging how likely a set of predictions is

acts.title: The Future of Work
tts: Phil Taylor has worked in recruitment in the UK and Australia, specializing in senior management.

I think the big change has been technology. In some industries it has shut things down; in others it has enhanced them and made them more profitable and more accessible. When I first started in recruitment, somebody who could write HTML code or build a website was quite a rare skill. Now it is part of a marketing person’s job, or part of an admin role.

Certainly ten years ago it was a very static work environment. You would come into the office and you would do your work from nine to five. Now companies are trying to be more creative with the workspace, and this is really to encourage the next generation of workers to choose them as their employer. So that would be things like working from your tablet in a coffee shop, or only needing to be in the office three days a week.

For the younger generation coming now, who are internet natives and used to being in a creative environment, I think it works very well. For more mature workers it may seem quite disruptive — not having their own set workspace, not having their own files around them, can be quite unsettling.
The challenge for businesses is not having all your staff in one place, and not having full visibility of their productivity on a day-to-day basis.

items.q: What does Phil say has been the biggest change?
o: Technology, which has shut some industries down and enhanced others

items.q: What was once a rare skill?
o: Writing HTML or building a website

items.q: How does he say younger and older workers differ?
o: Younger workers adapt easily; older ones may find it unsettling

items.q: What is the main challenge for businesses?
o: Not having staff in one place, and less visibility of productivity

acts.title: Grading how likely something is
rule: English grades likelihood far more finely than most languages, and at B2 the difference between “it will happen” and “it is bound to happen” is not emphasis — it is evidence. Saying something is bound to happen claims you can see why it must.
points: bound to, sure to, certain to. All take to + infinitive. It’s bound to happen.
likely to + infinitive, or I expect + clause. The verb be is compulsory: it is likely to rise.
may well, might well, could well. may well is stronger than plain may.
I doubt whether…, I wouldn’t be surprised if…, I suppose it might…
There’s no chance of + -ing. Note the -ing, not an infinitive.
eg: It’s bound to happen sooner or later.
Near-certain, with a reason implied.
That’s sure to happen.
Near-certain.
The figure is likely to rise by 2030.
Probable. be likely to — never “is likely rise”.
I expect they’ll travel more within their own countries.
Probable, personal judgement.
It may well become popular here too.
Possible, and stronger than plain may.
I doubt whether people would be satisfied with that.
Doubtful.
I wouldn’t be surprised if it happened.
Doubtful, but not ruled out. Note the past form after if.
Well, I suppose it might happen.
The weakest of all — reluctant agreement.
There’s no chance of me eating that.
Ruled out. no chance of + -ing.
People are more likely to be active if they live near green space.
Comparative form of likely.
acts.careful: “It is likely rise” and “There is no chance to eat that” are the two commonest errors here. likely takes to + infinitive; no chance of takes an -ing form.

acts.title: Should employers be able to require staff to work from the office?
parts: 1 · the question, and what the essay will do
text: Since 2020 a large number of employers have tried to bring staff back to the office full time, and almost as many have abandoned the attempt. This essay considers the arguments on both sides.

On the one hand, there are real reasons for wanting people in a building. Work that nobody has been asked to do — the overheard problem, the two-minute correction, the introduction between two colleagues who did not know they needed each other — is far more likely to happen when people share a space. Managers also point out that new staff learn a job largely by watching, and that this is very hard to replicate over a video call.

On the other hand, the costs fall unevenly. An hour’s commute each way is ten hours a week, and it is paid for by the employee rather than the employer. For anybody with children, or with a disability that makes travel difficult, a mandatory office day is not a preference but a barrier.

The two arguments are not equally easy to fix. The learning problem is real, but it can be solved with structure: fixed overlap days, deliberate pairing, protected time. The commute cannot be solved at all.

On balance, the evidence suggests that a requirement to attend is bound to produce resentment unless it comes with a stated purpose. Two fixed days for a named reason are defensible. Five days because a building exists are not.

items.r: states the question and what the essay will do
gives the case for, with concrete examples
gives the case against, taken seriously
weighs the two against each other
reaches a conclusion, with a condition attached

write.q: Write a balanced opinion essay of about 250 words on a question people where you work or study actually disagree about. Follow the model: state the question → the case for, with concrete examples → the case against, taken seriously → weigh the two → conclude, with a condition if you need one. Use at least three of the likelihood expressions from this lesson.
plan: the question, and what the essay will do
write.model:
Every few years somebody proposes that our company should stop advertising entirely and rely on referrals. This essay considers both sides of that argument.

On the one hand, the case is stronger than it sounds. Roughly half our best clients over the last four years came from somebody who already worked with us, and those clients stay measurably longer. A referred client arrives already convinced, which shortens the sales cycle from about six weeks to about ten days. Money spent on advertising is, by comparison, very hard to trace to anything.

On the other hand, referrals are not a channel; they are a result. They arrive when they arrive, and they are bound to reflect the clients we already have. A business that lives on referrals grows in one direction only, and I doubt whether we would ever have entered the two markets that now pay for everything else.

The two arguments are not the same kind of argument. The first is about cost per client, which is measurable. The second is about risk, which is not, and which only becomes visible in the year it goes wrong.

On balance I would keep advertising, but I would stop pretending it is a growth channel. It is likely to keep costing more than it returns in any single quarter. What it buys is the option to be somewhere new, and that option is only worth anything before you need it.
